title: The Shuffled Split

scenario.situation: The sales forecasting model validated with random k-fold CV shows a strong R² of 0.91 and low MAE in testing, but since deployment it has consistently underperformed — missing actuals by 20–30% and surprising the sales team every month.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team believes the model is fundamentally sound and that production lag is caused by noisy input data from the CRM or a recent shift in market conditions.
scenario.question: Why does a model that validated so well perform so poorly in production?

decisions.prompt: The team is ready to clean up CRM data and retrain on a larger dataset. How do you frame the investigation before touching anything?

options.label: Audit the CRM data pipeline for input noise
options.detail: Trace the features from source to model to find dirty or delayed data fields.
options.consequence: You spend a week auditing the pipeline and find minor data-quality issues — nothing that accounts for a 20–30% miss. The real problem remains invisible because you never questioned the validation methodology itself.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's hypothesis and investigated inputs while the flaw lived in the evaluation design.

options.label: Interrogate the validation methodology before touching data or features
options.detail: Ask whether the CV setup could have produced an optimistic score even on a weak model — check for any structural mismatch between how the model was validated and how it is used in production.
options.consequence: You immediately surface a structural question: the model is always predicting future sales from past signals, but k-fold randomly scrambles time. This framing points straight at the real driver without any new data collection.

options.label: Collect more recent data and retrain
options.detail: Assume market drift is real and expand the training window with the latest months.
options.consequence: The retrained model still validates at R² 0.90 and still underperforms in production by a similar margin. You've reproduced the same flawed loop at higher cost.
options.divergenceCost: Reran the broken experiment with fresher data — the flaw in the evaluation design repeated itself.

options.label: Compare feature importances to business intuition
options.detail: Review which features the model relies on most and ask the sales team if those make sense.
options.consequence: The features look reasonable to the sales team, reinforcing confidence in the model. The root cause — a leaky validation split — is invisible to feature-importance analysis.
options.divergenceCost: Validated model logic with domain intuition while the real issue was in the evaluation procedure, not the features.

decisions.prompt: You suspect the validation setup may be inflating scores. Which evaluation result do you trust to confirm or refute the model's true predictive power?

artifact.title: Model CV scores — random k-fold (5 folds)
artifact.caption: All five random folds score above 0.89. Impressive — but each fold's training set contains rows from dates that fall after some of the rows it predicts.

options.label: Random k-fold R² (the existing result)
options.detail: Use the five-fold cross-validated R² of ~0.91 already in the model card.
options.consequence: The 0.91 R² looks decisive, but random folds allow the model to train on January data while predicting the previous October — effectively peeking at the future. The metric measures memorization across time, not genuine forward forecasting ability.
options.divergenceCost: Trusted a metric whose data-splitting procedure violates the temporal order the model faces in production.

options.label: Time-ordered walk-forward CV R² (re-evaluated)
options.detail: Re-run CV using forward-chaining splits: train on months 1–N, predict month N+1; expand and repeat. Compute R² only on out-of-time folds.
options.consequence: Walk-forward CV exposes the true signal: R² drops to 0.54 on average and the latest folds — the ones most like production — score as low as 0.41. The gap between 0.91 and 0.54 is the exact fingerprint of future-data leakage through random splits.

artifact.title: Model R² — walk-forward time-ordered CV (same model)
artifact.caption: Performance degrades as the prediction horizon approaches production conditions. The most recent period — closest to live deployment — scores 0.41, versus the 0.91 claimed by random k-fold.

decisions.prompt: Walk-forward CV reveals R² of ~0.54 versus the reported 0.91. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "The model is broken because of future data leakage — scrap it and rebuild with time-ordered splits."
options.detail: Make a definitive diagnosis and prescribe immediate replacement.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified the validation flaw, but 'scrap it' overstates certainty. The model's architecture may be salvageable; the problem is the evaluation design, not necessarily every modelling choice. Acting without a controlled comparison risks discarding genuinely useful signal.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed by collapsing a validation-design finding into a verdict on the whole model.

options.label: "Random k-fold inflated scores by allowing future rows into training — walk-forward CV shows true out-of-time R² is ~0.54 and declining. We should retrain the same architecture under time-ordered splits and benchmark it against a naive baseline before deciding next steps."
options.detail: Report the finding, name the mechanism, and recommend a controlled next step rather than full replacement.
options.consequence: The team understands why the gap exists, not just that it exists. Proposing a retrain under correct splits — plus a naive baseline — gives a decision-ready benchmark without prematurely discarding the modelling work already done.

insight: The model was never as good as it looked: random k-fold let future rows leak into training, inflating R² from a true ~0.54 to a fictitious 0.91. The production gap wasn't noisy CRM data or market drift — it was the evaluation procedure systematically violating the temporal order the model faces in the real world. The lesson is structural: for any temporal forecasting task, validation splits must respect time, and walk-forward (forward-chaining) CV is the minimum credible standard. A strong analyst questions the measurement instrument before questioning the data.
